nodes.name: On any workflow error
nodes.notes: Every other workflow names this one as its Error Workflow, by the fixed id in its settings, so importing is enough and nobody has to remember to set it six times in the UI. This is the net under the net: the error outputs inside a workflow catch the failures somebody thought about, and this catches the ones nobody did -- a Code node throwing, Postgres refusing a connection, the container being OOM-killed mid-run.

parameters.query:
INSERT INTO dead_letters
  (workflow_id, workflow_name, execution_id, execution_url, node, kind,
   payload, attempts, error, reason)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7::jsonb, 1, $8, $9)
RETURNING id;

nodes.name: Dead letter
nodes.notes: Written before the alert is sent, not after. If the alert channel is down the failure is still recorded, and a dead letter with no alert is recoverable; an alert with no dead letter is a message about something you can no longer find.

parameters.query:
-- How many times this same workflow has crashed in the last fifteen minutes,
-- this one included.
--
-- An outage does not fail once. The provider goes down at 02:00, six
-- workflows crash every six hours until 09:00, and the person on call wakes
-- up to forty identical messages and a habit of muting the channel. That
-- habit is what actually takes the next outage from ten minutes to a day.
SELECT count(*)::int AS recent
FROM dead_letters
WHERE workflow_id = $1
  AND reason = 'crashed'
  AND created_at > now() - interval '15 minutes';

nodes.name: First one in 15 minutes?
nodes.notes: One message per workflow per fifteen minutes. The suppressed failures are not lost -- they are rows in dead_letters, and 06 health digest counts every one of them in the morning. Suppressing the alert and suppressing the record are very different things, and only one of them is safe.

nodes.name: Alert
nodes.notes: onError continue: this workflow must not be able to fail. An error workflow that throws does not get its own error workflow -- the failure just disappears.
